entry.title: The Age of Personal Software in Healthcare
entry.content:
I've been thinking about what personal software could mean for healthcare.

Imagine being able to describe a small tool you need and have an AI help you build it. Something that arranges your medical history in a way you understand. A dashboard that follows your lab results over time. An application that helps you prepare questions before an appointment.

You might use it for years. You might replace it next month.

But where does it get your medical history?

That question keeps bringing me back to what we are building with Merdra.

You can build a beautiful interface and still spend hours searching for old results, uploading documents, and explaining the same history again. If your information is scattered across hospitals, laboratories, paper files, and messages, creating another application does not automatically bring it together.

The software might be personal. The data it needs is still somewhere else.

A future of personal software would make this problem more visible. If more people can create the tools they want, more of those tools will need a reliable way to work with information that already exists.

Consider a simple example.

You want an application that displays your lab results over time. You give it permission to retrieve the relevant records, and it builds a timeline. Each result includes when the sample was collected, the unit, the reference range supplied by the lab, and where the result came from.

A few months later, you decide you want a different interface. Perhaps you prefer a local application on your laptop. Perhaps you want an agent to help organise your history before an appointment.

You should be able to make that change without reconstructing your medical history from scratch.

But why would anyone want to do this?

Honestly, building and maintaining your own health software sounds like a lot of work. Most people probably want something that already works. They do not want another project to manage.

Still, I can imagine cases where a person's needs are specific enough to make it worthwhile. Someone might want a simple timeline of results from different laboratories. Another might want an accessible interface in their preferred language. Someone managing a long-term condition might want to organise information around the questions they regularly discuss with their doctor.

They would not necessarily build these tools themselves.

This is the direction I want us to prepare Merdra for: patient-data infrastructure that different applications can work with, under appropriate permissions.

We cannot predict every useful piece of software someone will want. I don't think we need to. We need to think carefully about what those tools should be able to rely on.

One of those things is the source of a record.

A result issued by a laboratory, a symptom someone enters themselves, and an explanation generated by an AI are different kinds of information. A useful system should preserve those differences as information moves between applications.

If an agent produces a summary, someone should be able to trace it back to the records it used. If a laboratory corrects a result, applications should have a way to discover that correction. An old copy should not quietly appear to be the latest version.

Making information easier to move also means being more precise about permission.

Someone might want to let an application read their lab results without giving it access to every other part of their medical history. They might allow access for a week, or allow it to receive new results until they turn that permission off.

An application acting on a patient's behalf should only receive information that patient is permitted to access and authorised to share.

An agent acting for a patient should have a defined scope of access. It should be possible to see what it accessed and stop future access. That still leaves a difficult question about copies: revoking permission cannot magically erase information an external application has already downloaded.

These details become part of the product. They shape whether people can trust the software they connect.

Then there is security.

Every additional application that receives medical information creates another place where that information could be exposed. Patient permission alone would not make the connection safe.

We would need to consider how applications identify themselves, how little information they actually need, how access is recorded, and how it can be stopped. Patients should be able to understand what they are granting without needing to understand the infrastructure underneath it.

There is another boundary worth keeping clear: access to trustworthy records does not make an application clinically trustworthy.

An application can retrieve an authentic result and interpret it badly. An agent can cite the right document and still reach the wrong conclusion. Merdra's infrastructure would need to preserve evidence and accountability, while the software built on top would still need evaluation appropriate to what it does.

That matters to how I think about our own role.

We can build patient interfaces and explore medical agents. But I don't want the usefulness of the underlying infrastructure to depend on everyone choosing our interface.

Someone else may build a better experience for a particular person, language, or need. A patient may prefer a simpler tool. A developer may create something we would never have considered.

I want those possibilities to have somewhere reliable to start.

A useful early test would be whether an independently built application can connect with permission, retrieve results, preserve their context, and respond when something changes. It should also stop retrieving data when its access is revoked.

That is a smaller problem than supporting every imaginable medical agent, but it would tell us something real about the foundation we are building.

How much of this becomes part of everyday healthcare remains to be seen. Some people will keep choosing established products. Others may want tools built around their own routines.

For now, I'm just imagining what that future might look like.

entry.title: Thinking with AI
entry.content:
After publishing Taste in Software, I read Addy Osmani's Critical thinking when agents do the work.

He describes how delegating a task can gradually become accepting an answer without examining it. Two of his suggestions felt familiar: form an initial hypothesis before asking, and seek counterarguments from different models.

Those are things I already find myself doing. His article helped me understand why I want to keep doing them. It also left me with a question: if we increasingly ask humans to direct agents and judge their work, how do those humans learn to judge?

Writing gives me something to question

A small example is a note I was making for someone in real estate. It was basic: a list of the people a property platform would connect, including agents, renters, buyers, and owners. I wrote down responsibilities such as verification, trust, accountability, and management.

I needed to write it because I was still trying to think through the idea. Putting the pieces on the page gave me something I could rearrange and question.


That sketch was not yet a testable hypothesis, but it helped me move towards one. Perhaps people would choose the platform because it takes responsibility for verification. What would make them trust those checks? Who would be accountable when something goes wrong? What evidence would show that this matters to them?

I can explore those questions with a model, then test the assumptions with people in the market. Writing first gives me an initial position that can change. Otherwise, I may spend the whole exchange reacting to a polished proposal without making my own assumptions explicit.

Thinking with different models

Addy also describes asking more than one model to argue the opposite side of an open-ended question, then reviewing the arguments and forming his own opinion.

I recognise that in my conversations with Grok, Codex, and Claude. Moving an idea between them gives me opportunities to encounter an objection or framing I had not considered.

For the real estate idea, I could ask why owners and agents might avoid the platform, or how its incentives could undermine the trust it promises to provide.

Several models can still share the same weak assumption. Their agreement does not establish that an idea will work, and a persuasive objection still needs examination. I have to decide which arguments matter and what evidence would change my position.

The useful part is leaving the exchange better able to explain what I think and why.

The experience behind the workflow

An experienced engineer might delegate an implementation, choose a few important checks, and approve the result. Someone watching can copy those steps without understanding why those checks were chosen.

In my earlier article, I wrote:

We see what an experienced person can stop doing but ignore what they had to do before they could stop.

Consider a background job that sends an email. A request times out, so an agent adds a retry and a test showing that a failed attempt is followed by a successful one. Everything passes.

But the service may have accepted the first email before its response was lost. Retrying could send it twice. The test checked the behaviour we requested while leaving that possibility unexamined.

Someone has to notice the assumption. They might learn to recognise it through a mentor, documentation, an experiment, or a previous failure. Copying a workflow does not automatically transfer that experience.

Keeping room for practice

Practice can change as the tools improve. I do not think everyone needs to repeat the exact path taken by earlier generations of programmers. I want to know which lessons still matter and how a new workflow can teach them.

Before running generated code, I could predict its behaviour for a few inputs. After reading an explanation, I could close it and apply the idea to a different case. When an agent fixes a bug, I could reproduce the failure and work through why the change addresses it.

An agent can help with these exercises and suggest assumptions I missed. I still need opportunities to discover where my understanding falls short.

Teams need to make time for that learning too. If every task rewards the quickest delivery, investigating an unfamiliar part of a system becomes difficult to justify. Yet we may later expect the same person to diagnose failures and review important changes.

For me, writing before asking is one way to stay involved. Taking an idea to different models is another, provided I examine their arguments and seek evidence beyond their responses.

I want to leave an exchange able to say what changed in my understanding, and why. If human judgment is going to remain part of the workflow, people need room to develop it while the work is getting done.

November reads

While writing this, I also read a few of Addy’s other articles. See November Reads.

entry.title: Restyling This Site With Codex
entry.content:
I am not really a frontend or UI person, but I do know how things work there.

I can tell when something feels wrong on a page, but that does not mean I always know the CSS responsible for it. This site is personal, though, so I care about how it feels. I want it to be simple, calm, and centred on the things I write.

I recently restyled it with Codex using GPT-5.6 Sol at high reasoning effort.

It started with a question about SEO. Then I noticed inconsistent spacing, duplicated CSS, mobile problems, and pages that did not feel related. What began as a review slowly became a restyling of almost the entire site.

I did not begin with a finished design or a detailed reconstruction plan. I moved through the site one page at a time. I questioned new files, asked why styles were duplicated, compared mobile screenshots, and sometimes reversed changes that felt like too much. The design emerged through those small decisions rather than from one large redesign.

Trying not to overdo it

An AI coding agent makes it very easy to add things. A page can quickly gain cards, borders, gradients, animations, and another stylesheet.

That speed is useful, but it can also produce too much design.

Some early changes looked cool but stopped feeling like my website. The About page was one example. It had more personality, but it also felt over-designed. I kept giving the same feedback:

Tone it down a bit.

Codex could produce and modify the interface quickly, while I decided what actually belonged. We would add something, look at it, and remove the parts that made the page feel busy.

The goal was never to turn the site into a modern landing page. I wanted a slightly better version of what was already here.

Minimal as a system

I started to think of minimalism as having fewer rules to remember, not just fewer things on the screen.

Links are blue and turn green when hovered. Writings, Notes, Paper, and their archives use the same visual language. Dates, tags, headings, lists, and the little cd navigation should not look as if they came from unrelated websites.

This meant sharing templates, using the existing Sass structure, removing duplicated code, and checking the same layouts on desktop and mobile. A new page can now inherit an existing pattern instead of needing its own design and stylesheet.

That is more useful to me than making one page impressive on its own.

The Daveads Galaxy

The biggest addition was the Daveads Galaxy: Daveads at the centre, categories as constellations, topics as planets, and articles inside them.

I did not want it to be a hardcoded visual that would break as I wrote more. It reads the categories and tags already used by Writings and Notes. When I publish something new, the Galaxy should understand where it belongs without me manually adding another planet.

Mobile made the feature more interesting. Planets needed useful touch targets. Tapping one had to reveal its articles. Zooming the Galaxy should not zoom the entire page, and the navigation still needed to work in full-screen mode. We also kept a list view for anyone who wants a simpler way to browse.

The Galaxy is more playful than the rest of the website, but it follows the same rule: content should drive the interface.

Working with Codex

A lot of my feedback came through screenshots. I would notice too much empty space, an uncentred video, a heading disappearing on mobile, or two labels sitting too close together. I could point at the problem without knowing which template or Sass rule created it.

Codex could trace the element back to the code and make a focused change. I would look at the result and decide whether it felt right. That loop worked well for someone who is not a frontend person but still has an opinion about the result.

We also checked the less visible things: responsiveness, builds, internal links, test pages, the Atom feed, and whether Google Analytics remained untouched.

After experimenting, we refactored the Galaxy into smaller files and shared common code across other pages. Generated code can work while still being difficult for a human to own. I want to open the repository later, find the relevant file, and change it myself.

GPT-5.6 Sol at high reasoning effort was helpful when a small request crossed templates, Sass, JavaScript, content configuration, and mobile behaviour. The official OpenAI documentation describes high effort as useful for complex planning, debugging, and agentic work, which matched this project.

But it did not replace taste. I still had to say when something was too much, protect the parts I liked, and ask whether a new file was really necessary.

Codex gave me implementation speed. I kept responsibility for what the website should feel like.

The site now has more capability, but its ordinary pages feel calmer and more consistent. More importantly, it still feels like mine.
